opus-5.5.text:
Part of it is that the system isn't just one model thinking harder. It's structured more like a scientific community. Different agents play different roles. Some generate hypotheses, some critique them, some rank them against each other in what's essentially a tournament, and some take the strongest ideas and try to refine or combine them. When you give it more compute, you're not just letting one agent ramble longer. You're running more rounds of that generate, debate and evolve loop.

The key ingredient is that the system has some internal signal of quality. In the tournament, ideas are compared head to head and get something like an Elo rating. So as you spend more computation, you explore more of the space of possible hypotheses, and you also have a mechanism to filter and improve them. The good ideas survive and get refined, and the weak ones get pushed down. That's quite similar to how science works at a societal level. Many people propose things, peers critique them, and over time the better explanations rise.

What was striking for us was that the quality kept improving with more test-time compute, as judged both by the system's own ratings and by human experts. That suggests self-critique and comparison really add value beyond the raw capability of the underlying model. Of course, the internal rating isn't ground truth. Ultimately you need experimental validation, and that's why we worked with labs to actually test some of these hypotheses. In several cases, the ideas the system ranked highly turned out to hold up in the lab, which gives us some confidence that the scaling is real and not just the system flattering itself.

r001.rationale: The response says quality improves with more test-time computation, but does not say this continues even when computation is extended to days.

r002.rationale: It describes exploring more hypotheses, but does not suggest that valuable insights may lie in the low-probability tail of the model’s proposal distribution.

r003.rationale: It describes agents that critique, rank, and refine ideas, but does not claim Gemini evaluates proposed ideas better than it generates them.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that co-scientist is really a search process, and the thing that makes it work is that we built in a way to evaluate and compare ideas, not just generate them.

So the system has a set of agents. There's a generation agent that proposes hypotheses, grounded in the literature. But then there's a reflection agent that critiques those hypotheses, a ranking agent that runs essentially a tournament between them, where it has these debates and uses an Elo-style rating to figure out which ideas are winning, and an evolution agent that takes the strong ideas and tries to refine them, combine them, simplify them. And there's a supervisor orchestrating all of this.

Now, the reason more compute helps is that this is an iterative loop. In the first round you have a bunch of hypotheses, many of them are mediocre. If you only run one round, that's what you get. But if you keep going, the tournament keeps identifying the best candidates, the evolution step keeps improving them, and the critiques feed back into the next round of generation. So you're climbing. We actually measured this: as you increase test-time compute, the Elo ratings of the top hypotheses keep going up, and importantly, when we had expert scientists blindly judge the outputs, their assessments of novelty and impact tracked that Elo signal. So the self-evaluation isn't just the system flattering itself, it correlates with what domain experts think.

I'd say the deeper point is that this is the same lesson we've seen in other systems: if you can turn a problem into something with a reasonable verifier or comparison mechanism, you can trade compute for quality. In AlphaGo the verifier was the game outcome. Here we don't have a perfect verifier for a scientific idea, but we have a pretty good proxy in structured debate and critique, and that proxy is good enough that search over it actually finds better ideas. That's what you're seeing with the scaling.

r001.rationale: The response says quality improves with more test-time computation and additional rounds, but does not say that improvement continues over days.

r002.rationale: It describes searching, ranking, and refining hypotheses, but does not suggest that valuable insights are in the low-probability tail of the model’s proposal distribution.

r003.rationale: It describes separate generation and evaluation agents, but does not claim that Gemini is better at evaluating ideas than generating them.

astra-6.text:
The intuition is that you’re giving the system more opportunity to propose ideas, critique them, and refine them. It’s not just generating a single answer and stopping. Different agents can explore different hypotheses, while others examine those hypotheses for weaknesses or compare competing explanations. That feedback can then inform the next round of proposals.

So additional computation can support a richer search: explore more possibilities, spend more time evaluating the promising ones, and combine or revise ideas based on the critiques. The important distinction is that more computation doesn’t automatically make an idea correct. It can make the hypothesis better developed and more worth testing, but ultimately you still need experiments to establish whether it’s right.

sol-6.1.text:
The intuition is that you’re giving the system more opportunity to explore ideas and then be critical of them. It isn’t just generating one answer and stopping. Different agents can propose hypotheses, critique them, compare them, and use that feedback to refine them or explore a different direction.

So additional computation lets that process go further: you can consider more candidates and spend more effort examining the promising ones. The important thing is that the computation is being used for an iterative search, with feedback, rather than simply producing a longer answer.

Of course, a hypothesis that survives that process still needs to be tested experimentally. The system’s role is to help scientists find more promising ideas to test.

r002.rationale: It discusses exploring more candidates, but does not suggest valuable insights may lie in the low-probability tail of the model’s proposals.
